title: How I Actually Make Time for Things I Care About
author: Amir Satvat
source: Level Up with Ethan Evans (levelupwithethanevans.substack.com), October 27, 2026
summary: In this guest post for Ethan Evans and Jason Yoong's newsletter, Amir Satvat explains how he runs ASGC, a free volunteer-powered career community for the games industry, alongside a full-time job and three young children. Evans pressed him to separate what is unusual about his stamina from what anyone could copy, and the result is six practices, each closed with a short list of actionable steps. He begins with a fanatical interest in the cause, backs it with real effort, and plans weekly and monthly time in a spreadsheet so that he knows early when the math does not work. He is deliberate about what he gives up, takes breaks without guilt, and keeps putting himself out there so that other people can help. The tone is candid that nobody should copy his schedule. His broader advice is to start with one small problem, give it a sustainable number of hours, tell a few people and keep going, instead of trying to change the world. The piece suits leaders who want a realistic model for protecting time for work that matters beyond their day job.
points: Sustained extra effort depends on a cause you would work on for free, because a lukewarm interest rated seven out of ten will not survive tired evenings.
Writing out one real week, with family, work and sleep first, shows what time is actually left and lets you decide early when the plan does not fit.
Time for a new commitment must come from somewhere, so identify the activity you do mostly out of habit and cut it, but do not cut things you love just to look productive.
A structured plan works best when it is forgiving, since resting when needed keeps a four-year effort alive longer than a perfect two-month sprint.
Telling five people what you are working on and asking for something specific brings in help, and making the problem the point keeps visibility from becoming vanity.
quotes: I honestly don’t think I could do this amount of work for something where my interest level was like a 7 out of 10.
People sometimes see something after four years and assume there was some giant moment where it suddenly became what it is. That has not been my experience. Most things are boringly incremental.
I would rather know on Sunday that the math doesn’t work than find out on Thursday after feeling like I am failing at everything.

There is no productivity book that is going to give you a second Thursday, so if you want to add five hours of something to your life, you either had five empty hours already or something else now has to get five fewer hours.
My approach is extremely structured and also forgiving when it needs to be. Those things sound contradictory, but for me they aren’t.
I would much rather do something imperfectly for four years than do it perfectly for two months and hate it.
You can be visible for the sake of your cause without making yourself the point, and that distinction is important to me. Make the problem the point.
You do not need to change the world. Helping somebody is already good, and then helping somebody else is even better.
